context: Wilde to Frank Harris, Saturday [18 February 1899], Hotel Terminus, Nice. Three days after the letter begging for £20, thanking him for sending it. The money talk brackets the most considered self-defence in the Harris correspondence — 'such a gap between the two Oscars', and 'only the utterly worthless can be reformed'.
quote:
Sebastian Melmoth

Hotel Terminus, Nice. Saturday.

My dear Frank, Many, many thanks for your enclosure and letter. The hotel had become perfectly brutal, as I had not been able to pay them anything.

I hope you don’t really think I had forgotten about the money you so kindly gave me in Paris — but that I spent before coming down in paying my hotel and other bills. I was only alluding to what you had given me since our arrival, nine weeks ago. And I trust you don’t think I have rushed you too much, or been recklessly extravagant.

I have again written to Smithers, my publisher, to ask him to let me have something on account of my play, just published; which I think he can hardly refuse doing: tho’ I do not fancy the play will have anything like the success of the ‘Ballad’. It is so trivial, so irresponsible a comedy: and while the public like to hear of my pain — curiosity and the autobiographical form being elements of interest — I am not sure that they will welcome me again in airy mood, and spirit mocking at morals, and defiance of social rules. There is, or at least in their eyes there should be, a gap between the two Oscars — I believe they would like me to edit prayers for those at sea, or to recant the gospel of Life in a penny tract. They do not see that only the utterly worthless can be reformed. Permanence of temperament — the indomitable assertion of the soul (and by soul I mean the unity of mind and body —) — such are the things of value in anyone.

In the meanwhile I want to get out of the hotel — the prices are appalling — and for the past four days I have been obliged to have my meals there — loathsome German cooking — at 10 francs a day — _rien compris_ — and my bedroom still at almost carnival prices —: Of course when I went there I thought you would be moving into a villa at once — as you yourself did too. I gave them 200 francs this morning. But I owe nearly 100 francs more. If you could kindly lend me this, I would return it to you next week, when I am sure Smithers will let me have at least a tenner. There is a capital little hotel — in the Rue d’Angleterre — where I can get pension, with room, for 8 francs a day —: in the Hotel Terminus I feel living in a White Elephant, and being obliged to feed the monster. When I stayed there before I was Mellor’s guest, so I did not know how horribly dear it was. I am sure, if you can, you will do this. I must get out of the place at once.

I am delighted to see you won your libel action — but what a bore those things are — and what a bore, the [man?] —

Ever O.W.
original_provenance: Read at HRC 2676, images 56-57 - one sheet of Grand Cafe Glacier, Nice paper (Levet & Rinino), squared stock, written both sides; image 56 is the recto, 57 the verso, the letterhead showing through mirrored at its head. Heading: 'Sebastian Melmoth', ruled off, above the address - the third appearance of the exile name in this cluster, after p. 1029 and the Smithers telegram of the same week. The volume drops it and heads the letter 'Hotel Terminus, Nice'. Emphasis: one underline, '_rien compris_', running across the line break - 'rien' at the end of one line and 'compris' at the head of the next both carry it, so it is a single mark on the phrase and not a line-break artefact. It complicates the french rule: he underlined this French, where he did not underline 'sans le sou' (p. 1123) or 'Rien n'est sacre a un cocher de fiacre' (Ives, p. 1173). The volume italicises all three identically. So its italic on French is uninformative in both directions - it neither proves a mark nor rules one out, and only the sheet decides. Null: 'Permanence of temperament' is not underlined, checked at 3x - it reads emphatic because he writes it larger, not because it is marked. The squared ruling of this stock fakes underlines freely; every mark here was taken at 2.6-3x. Title: 'the ‘Ballad’' - his inverted commas, and note the article is outside them and lower case. The volume prints 'The Ballad' in italic, which silently moves the article inside the title. Fifth instance of the quotes-to-italic conversion. The last line, which the volume does not print, in `manuscripts/hrc/2676-wilde-to-harris/page-57-2643.jpg`. The edition ends the letter at 'what a bore those things are.' - confirmed on a whole-page render, with the next heading following, so it really does stop there. The sheet goes on: 'and what a bore, the [man?] —' followed by his usual Ever-yours squiggle and 'O.W.' Reading: '[man?]', Lovelle's, queried for the smudge. Three letters, the second being his 'a', with an ink smudge across it. The sense corroborates it independently: the libel action Wilde is congratulating Harris on is Yeatman's, and the volume's own footnote records that 'the plaintiff conducted his own case' before Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and a special jury. Yeatman sued in person and lost, so 'what a bore those things are - and what a bore, the man' has an obvious referent. Kept queried rather than silently resolved, because the smudge is real. The queried word is a doubtful reading, not a gap, so the quote is complete and `marks_verified` is set. There is no underlining anywhere on this side, so nothing about the mark record turns on it. (Contrast p. 1206, which stays withheld because three passages there are genuinely unread.)
